prompt: To make the planner faster, a teammate sets the host to send `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` on every file it serves, `index.html` included. What happens, after today's deploy, to a student who last visited a week ago?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 1.

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong: the new build's scripts carry new hashed names, so her browser fetches them on its next visit
choices.why: The new names are only found through the new `index.html`, and her browser is using last week's copy of it without asking anybody.

choices.text: Her browser sends `If-None-Match` for the page, gets a 200 with the new HTML, and then fetches the new scripts
choices.why: A fresh copy is used with no request at all, and `immutable` skips the check even on a reload. A conditional request only happens once a copy is stale.

choices.text: Her browser keeps last week's `index.html` for up to a year, and that page keeps naming last week's scripts
choices.why: The page is the one file that carries the new names, which is why it is sent `no-cache` and checked every time. Kept for a year, it holds her on the old release.

choices.text: The CDN serves her the new page at once, because a deploy replaces the whole folder on the host
choices.why: A deploy changes what the host holds, not what sits on her disk. A CDN can be purged; a visitor's browser cannot.

prompt: In a review you find `fetchPolicy: "no-cache"` on the planner's main query. Its author explains: "like the HTTP header, it keeps the answer and checks with the server every time." What do the two lessons say?
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 10; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: Both keep and revalidate; Apollo's policy simply checks with a fresh query where HTTP sends `If-None-Match`
choices.why: Apollo's `no-cache` always asks the server and keeps nothing, so there is no copy to revalidate.

choices.text: The names match and the meanings differ: Apollo's `no-cache` stores nothing, which is nearer to HTTP's `no-store`
choices.why: HTTP's `no-cache` means keep it and ask before using it. In Apollo's table `no-cache` asks every time and keeps nothing; the policy that asks and still writes the cache is `network-only`.

choices.text: Apollo's `no-cache` is `cache-first` with a short lifetime, after which it asks the server for what expired
choices.why: `cache-first` answers from the cache without asking when every field is there. `no-cache` never reads the cache at all.

choices.text: HTTP's `no-cache` keeps nothing either, so the comparison holds and the policy does what its author wants
choices.why: That is the confusion web-fundamentals warns about: `no-cache` asks, `no-store` refuses. HTTP's `no-cache` does keep the copy.

prompt: Moving the planner to a new host, Ana points `www.example.com` at the new address. The record carries a TTL of 3600, and she did not lower it beforehand. At most how many minutes after her change can a resolver still hand out the old answer?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 4.

prompt: The planner moves to its own domain, `example.com`, on a host that gave the project the name `planner.pages.dev`. Match each need to the record that meets it.
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 4; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8.

pairs.right: `A`, with the addresses the host's documentation lists

pairs.left: the random string the host shows, to prove the domain is yours
the company's mail for addresses at `@example.com`
pairs.right: `MX`, naming a server and a priority

prompt: Ana runs the planner on a VPS of her own, with a Let's Encrypt certificate renewed automatically through the HTTP-01 challenge. Once every link used HTTPS, she closed port 80 at the firewall. Two months later the certificate expired, and the renewal job's log shows the challenge failing. Why?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 9; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 4.

choices.text: The authority asks for its file over plain HTTP, at `/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>`, and nothing answers there now
choices.why: HTTP-01 proves control of the name by serving a file over plain HTTP, so port 80 has to stay reachable. Closing it leaves the authority's question with no answer.

choices.text: HTTP-01 only issues the first certificate; renewals need a `TXT` record at `_acme-challenge`, which she never made
choices.why: Renewal answers the same question as the first issue, by the same challenge. DNS-01 is what a wildcard name needs, not what a renewal needs.

choices.text: A certificate obtained over HTTP covers `http://` addresses only, and a site served over HTTPS alone needs another kind
choices.why: A certificate binds a key to names, not to a scheme. The challenge is only how control of the name is proved.

choices.text: The renewal worked, but the web server kept the old certificate in memory because nothing told it to reload
choices.why: That failure is real and is a different one: the log would show a successful renewal. Here it shows the challenge failing.

prompt: Tidying the planner's rules, Ana deploys `/* /beta/:splat 301` by mistake, notices five minutes later and deploys the fix. A day later, some people who visited during those five minutes still land on `/beta/`. Why, and what would have kept the mistake short?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 4.

choices.text: Their resolvers cached the old rules for the record's TTL; lowering the TTL before deploying would have helped
choices.why: The rules file is read by the host on each request, not handed out by DNS. No resolver ever held it.

choices.text: The CDN still holds the old rules, and purging the edge right after the fix would have ended it for everybody
choices.why: The host applied the new rules at once. What remains is in each visitor's browser, and no purge reaches a browser.

choices.text: A `301` is followed once per visit, so the next visit reads the rules again and the fix reaches them then
choices.why: It is the other way round: browsers store a `301` without being told to, and the next visit goes straight to `/beta/` with no request.

choices.text: Their browsers stored the `301` and stopped asking; a `302` first would have kept the mistake short
choices.why: A permanent redirect is remembered, so nothing Ana serves reaches people who are not asking. A `302` is not remembered, and is the code to test with.

prompt: The planner answers on both `example.com` and `www.example.com`, with no redirect between them. A student signs in on `www.example.com`, follows a link to `example.com/course/git`, and is shown as signed out. What explains it, and what does front-delivery lesson 4 do about it?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 4.

choices.text: The session cookie is `SameSite=Strict`; switching it to `Lax` lets the link from one name to the other carry it
choices.why: `SameSite` decides which site may cause the cookie to be sent. Here the cookie does not belong to the other host at all, whatever its `SameSite` says.

choices.text: A cookie set without `Domain` goes back only to the host that set it; pick one name and 301 the other to it
choices.why: Left out, `Domain` ties the cookie to `www.example.com` exactly. Lesson 4 picks one address per page and redirects the other spelling, rather than widening the cookie.

choices.text: The two names carry two certificates, and a browser drops a session's cookies when the certificate changes
choices.why: Certificates say who answers for a name; they decide nothing about cookies. The cookie stayed on the name that set it.

choices.text: The apex has an `A` record and `www` a `CNAME`, and a browser keeps cookies apart by the record type behind a name
choices.why: The browser never sees record types. The two names are two hosts, and that alone keeps the cookie apart.

prompt: A team deleted its docs project on a static host and left `docs.example.com` as a `CNAME` to `example-docs.pages.dev`. Its main app sets the session cookie with `Domain=example.com`. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 4; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: Anybody who creates a project of that name on that host can serve pages at `docs.example.com`
choices.why: The record points at a name that is nobody's now, and the first to claim it answers for the subdomain: a subdomain takeover.

choices.text: Pages served there by a stranger are sent the app's session cookie, since `Domain=example.com` covers every subdomain
choices.why: A widened cookie goes to every subdomain, the abandoned one included. That is why web-fundamentals says to widen nothing without a reason.

choices.text: Deleting the `CNAME` first and the project second would have left nothing to take over
choices.why: A record pointing at nothing of yours is the hazard; a project with no record pointing at it is harmless.

choices.text: The app's valid certificate for `example.com` stops a stranger from serving pages under its subdomains
choices.why: The host obtains a certificate for whichever project the name points at. A certificate says who answers for a name, and here that would be the stranger.

choices.text: Lowering the record's TTL to sixty seconds closes the hole, because the stale answer stops being served quickly
choices.why: The TTL says how long an answer may be cached, not where it points. The current answer is the dangerous one.

prompt: In front-delivery lesson 10 the GraphQL server is stopped, and the dev server logs `http proxy error: /graphql` with `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4000`, while the page's request gets a 502. Reading that status the way web-fundamentals lesson 6 does, where is the fault?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 10.

choices.text: In the page: a 5xx is the answer to a request so malformed that the proxy could not read it
choices.why: A request the server cannot make sense of is a `400`, and a 4xx says the client asked wrong. A 5xx says the failure is on the server's side.

choices.text: In the proxy itself: a 502 means the dev server failed, and it is the one to restart first
choices.why: The dev server answered with the 502, so it is up. A 502 is a proxy reporting on what is behind it.

choices.text: Further back: the one that replied is fine, and whatever listens on 4000 is down
choices.why: A `502 Bad Gateway` is a proxy saying the thing behind it did not give a usable answer. The log names that thing: port 4000.

choices.text: Nowhere yet: the server is up and deliberately not serving, and will answer once the maintenance ends
choices.why: That describes a `503 Service Unavailable`. A 502 comes from a proxy, about the server behind it.

prompt: The planner's GraphQL server answers every request with a 200, failed queries included, and the team's dashboard counts failures by status code. Web-fundamentals lesson 6 lists what an error inside a 200 breaks. Which of those apply here? Choose all that apply.
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 9; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: The dashboard shows a healthy service while queries fail
choices.why: Software between the planner and its server looks only at the number, and the number is always 200.

choices.text: Code that checks only `response.ok` treats every failed query as a success
choices.why: `ok` reflects the status. Whether the query worked is in the body's `errors` list, which such code never reads.

choices.text: A client library that retries on a 5xx never retries a failed query
choices.why: A retry rule keyed on the status never fires, because no GraphQL failure here is a 5xx.

choices.text: A CDN in front of the API keeps a failed answer and serves it to everybody who asks the same query
choices.why: Every query is a `POST` to one address, and only `GET` and `HEAD` are cached in practice. That is also why HTTP caches do not help GraphQL.

choices.text: A typo in a field name still comes back as a 500, so at least typos reach the dashboard
choices.why: A query the schema refuses comes back with `errors` and no `data`, and with a 200 like everything else.

prompt: A site answers on `example.com` and on `www.example.com`, over `http` and over `https`, with and without a trailing slash, and redirects none of them to another. How many addresses does lesson 4 count for its home page?
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 4.

prompt: In review, a colleague points at the built `dist/index.html`, where `<script type="module" crossorigin src="/assets/index-BVi82VJx.js"></script>` sits in the `<head>`: "that stops the parser until the script has run; move it to the end of the body." What is the right answer?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 10; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 1.

choices.text: A module script behaves like `defer`: it is fetched while parsing goes on and runs once the document is parsed
choices.why: Only a plain `<script src>` stops the parser. In the head, a module is found early, fetched early, and run at the moment the end of the body would have run it.

choices.text: It does block, but the bundle is about 3 kB, so moving it would save too little to be worth a change
choices.why: The size is beside the point: a module script does not block the parser at all, whatever it weighs.

choices.text: It blocks today; adding `async` beside `crossorigin` fixes it and keeps the page's scripts in their order
choices.why: `async` runs a script the moment it arrives, interrupting parsing, and keeps no order. A module already waits for the parse.

choices.text: `crossorigin` already delays it until the body has been parsed, so the colleague's change would make no difference
choices.why: `crossorigin` says how the request is made, not when the script runs. What delays it is `type="module"`.

prompt: A pull request to `@planner/ui`, now at `0.2.0`, renames the token `muted` to `subtle` throughout the library and releases it as `0.2.1`. The library's own tests are green. What is wrong?
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lessons 5 and 7.

choices.text: Nothing: tokens are CSS rather than exports, so renaming one changes no interface and a patch is right
choices.why: A token's name is an interface. Every consumer's `var(--muted)` is now empty, silently, and no compiler says so.

choices.text: A breaking change went out as a patch: keep `muted` as a deprecated alias first, and remove it in `0.3.0`
choices.why: Renaming a token is a major change, and before `1.0.0` npm treats the minor as the breaking part. The alias keeps every product working until it has moved.

choices.text: It needs `1.0.0`: a rename is major, and the major part is the first number of every version, `0.x` included
choices.why: Before `1.0.0` the rules shift down one place, so `0.3.0` is the breaking release. `1.0.0` is the release that promises stability.

choices.text: A patch is fine here, provided consumers accept `^0.2.0` so that every product picks the rename up at once
choices.why: `^0.2.0` accepts `0.2.1`, which is exactly how the broken colours would reach every consumer automatically.

prompt: Months ago Ana pointed her domain's `NS` records at a new DNS provider. Today she adds the host's verification `TXT` record in the registrar's original DNS panel, which saves it without complaint. An hour later the host still cannot find it. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 4.

choices.text: She looked the name up before creating it, so resolvers hold a negative answer for as long as the `SOA` allows
choices.why: Negative caching is real, but asking the authoritative servers would still find no record: it was written where they do not read.

choices.text: A DNS change takes up to 48 hours to propagate, so the host has to keep checking until tomorrow
choices.why: Nothing propagates: a change takes as long as the old TTL. And this record never reached the servers that answer for the domain.

choices.text: A `TXT` record cannot sit under a name such as `_vercel.example.com`; it has to be at the bare domain
choices.why: Hosts ask for exactly such names, `_vercel.example.com` among them, and a `TXT` record may sit under any name.

choices.text: That panel stopped being authoritative when the `NS` moved, so nothing reads it
choices.why: After a change of nameservers the old panel still works and still saves, and is read by nobody. Check which servers are authoritative before editing anything.

prompt: The planner's server now sends an `etag` with each file. On the next visit, a browser holding a stale copy sends that tag back in the request header `___`, and a match is answered `304 Not Modified` with no body.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7; Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 9.

prompt: The planner ships front-performance lesson 10's service worker: cache first for `/assets/`, network first for pages. Today's deploy changes a page and a script and leaves `sw.js` as it was. Does a returning visitor need a new worker to see the change?
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 1; Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 10.

choices.text: Yes: cache first keeps serving the old script from the worker's cache until `CACHE` is renamed in `sw.js`
choices.why: Cache first is keyed by address, and the new build's script lives at a new address. The old one is simply never asked for again.

choices.text: Yes: until the worker's file differs by a byte, the browser does not ask the network for a page at all
choices.why: The byte rule is about the worker's own file. Its pages are network first, so a visitor online gets the page the server draws now.

choices.text: No: a page is fetched fresh while online, and the edited file now lives at an address nobody kept
choices.why: A build changes a file's name when it changes its content, and the new page names the new file. A new worker is needed only when the worker itself changes.

choices.text: No, but only once the visitor has closed every tab, because the old worker controls the ones still open
choices.why: Waiting is what a new version of the worker does. This deploy makes no new version, so there is nothing to wait for.

prompt: The planner is on Netlify with `/* /index.html 200` in its `_redirects`. After a deploy, error reports keep arriving, tagged with the previous release, about scripts the browser refused to run because of their MIME type. What is happening?
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lessons 4 and 11.

choices.text: Tabs opened before the deploy ask for their own build's files, and the catch-all answers each request with `index.html`
choices.why: The new release does not have those files, so the rewrite sends the page, as HTML with a 200, and the browser will not run it. Reports from an old release are those tabs, not a new bug.

choices.text: The deploy broke the host's `Content-Type` table, so every script of the new release now goes out as HTML
choices.why: The reports carry the previous release. The new build's own scripts exist, and are sent as JavaScript.

choices.text: Netlify applies rules before files, so `/*` swallows every real script; a `!` after the 200 is the fix
choices.why: Netlify applies a rule only when no file matches. The `!` forces a rule over real files, which would make it worse.

choices.text: The CDN still holds the previous release's scripts under an old `Content-Type`, and a purge would clear them
choices.why: The files the old tabs want are gone, not stale, so no edge holds a copy to serve.

prompt: Tomorrow the planner's `www` record moves to a new host, and it carries a TTL of a day. Put the steps in the order that makes the move take minutes.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 4.
items: Lower the TTL of the record to sixty seconds
Let at least one old TTL pass, so every copy of the old number has run out
Point the record at the new host
Check that the site works at its new home
Raise the TTL back to about a day
trap: The likeliest slip is lowering the TTL and changing the record at the same sitting. The lowering is itself held under the old TTL, so it has to be done at least that long before the move.

prompt: Ana committed `.env` with the support token in it, pushed to the team's private repository, and noticed an hour later. Put lesson 2's response in order.
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 2.
items: Replace the token at the service that issued it, and revoke the old one
Read the service's logs for what the old token did while it was out
Run `git rm --cached .env` and add `.env` to `.gitignore`
Rewrite the history with `git filter-repo` and force-push
trap: The likeliest slip is starting with git. No commit, removal or rewrite reaches the clones and scanners that already have the token; only replacing it at the service makes the leaked copy useless, private repository or not.

prompt: The planner's staging site still calls the old API. Somebody changed `VITE_GRAPHQL_URL` in the host's dashboard yesterday, and nobody has pushed since. What does lesson 2 say is going on?
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 2.

choices.text: The dashboard writes the new value into `.env.local` on the host, a file that only `npm run dev` reads
choices.why: The host does not edit files in the project. A variable set there is read by the build, and the build has not run since.

choices.text: The browser reads `import.meta.env` from the host when the page opens, and is still using yesterday's copy
choices.why: A browser has no environment to read. `import.meta.env.VITE_GRAPHQL_URL` was replaced by a literal string while the bundle was built.

choices.text: The last build wrote the old value into the bundle as a string; nothing changes until it is rebuilt
choices.why: In a front end a variable is read once, by the build. The host serves the old value until the next deploy builds the site with the new one.

choices.text: The host applies the new value at once, and the old answers come from the CDN's copy of the staging API
choices.why: Nothing about the API changed; the address the page calls is fixed inside the bundle it downloaded.

prompt: A preview found by a search engine competes with the real site. Cloudflare Pages keeps its previews out by adding the response header `X-Robots-Tag: ___` to their addresses.
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 3.

prompt: On CI, `npm ci` stops with `Invalid: lock file's typescript@6.0.3 does not satisfy typescript@6.0.2`. A teammate proposes deleting `package-lock.json` and committing that, so the build goes green. What is wrong with the plan?
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 3.

choices.text: Nothing, provided the workflow switches to `npm install`, which writes a fresh lockfile on every run
choices.why: Then CI installs whatever is newest on the day of each run, and checks code nobody committed. That is the thing `npm ci` exists to prevent.

choices.text: The CI cache is keyed by the lockfile's hash, so a missing lockfile leaves every later run without a cache
choices.why: A changed lockfile costs one slow run and then a warm cache. That is a small price, not what is wrong here.

choices.text: The lockfile is only a hint to npm, so deleting it changes nothing about the versions that get installed
choices.why: It is a hint to `npm install`. `npm ci` installs exactly what it records, which is why CI trusts it.

choices.text: It turns a pin into whatever is newest that day; the fix is to bring the two files into step through npm and commit both
choices.why: A deleted lockfile is regenerated with the newest versions available, the opposite of a pin. The lockfile changes only through npm, in the same commit as `package.json`.

prompt: A developer on a Mac runs the library's screenshot tests for the first time, and each one writes a new picture instead of comparing. The approved pictures in the repository end in `-chromium-linux.png`. What does lesson 6 recommend?
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 6.

choices.text: Make CI, on Linux, the one photographer, and update pictures through CI rather than from a laptop
choices.why: Pictures depend on the fonts, the browser build and the system that drew them. One machine approving them keeps one set that means something.

choices.text: Commit the new `-chromium-darwin.png` pictures as well, so that every system has an approved set of its own
choices.why: Two approved sets drift apart, and each is checked only on the machines that drew it, so a change can pass on one and never be seen.

choices.text: Raise the comparison's tolerance until the Mac's pictures and Linux's fall within it
choices.why: A tolerance wide enough to forgive another system forgives real changes too; the default already let a lighter grey through.

choices.text: Replace the Linux pictures with the Mac's, since a picture is approved by whoever ran the test last
choices.why: That swaps one photographer for another and makes CI fail on every run, because CI looks for the Linux names.

prompt: A page uses `<planner-session>`, whose button lives in an open shadow root and carries `part="button"`. Match each thing the page writes to what it does to the element or its button.
hint: Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 8.

pairs.right: nothing: the page's selectors stop at the shadow root
reaches it, like every other token in `tokens.css`
styles it, because the element named that piece
makes the row a block, winning over the element's `:host`

right_distractors: styles it only if the shadow root is `closed`
reaches it only once the element sets `composed: true`

prompt: A product page's field data says its CLS is 0.18 on phones and 0.03 on desktops. The paragraph under the hero is what moves. The hero is ``, styled `width: 100%; height: auto;`. Which change to the markup removes the cause?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 4; Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 5.

choices.text: Add `loading="lazy"`, so on a phone the picture stops competing with the text for the connection
choices.why: Lazy loading makes a picture arrive while somebody is reading, by design. Without its room reserved that is still a shift, and on the hero it delays the LCP as well.

choices.text: Add `fetchpriority="high"`, so the picture arrives before the text has been painted
choices.why: Priority changes when the request starts, not how much room the box takes. On a slow network the picture still lands after the first paint, and the paragraph still jumps.

choices.text: Add `width` and `height` in the file's proportions, so its height is known before it arrives
choices.why: The browser reads the two attributes as a ratio, and with `height: auto` it works out the height from the width before a byte of the file has come. The paragraph is placed below that room and never moves. Phones score worse because the same shift covers more of a small window.

choices.text: Offer smaller files in `srcset`, so the picture is in before the reader reaches the paragraph
choices.why: A smaller file arrives sooner and still arrives after the layout. With no size kept for it, the box goes from 0 tall to its full height and pushes the paragraph down.

prompt: To save mobile data, a teammate adds a lint rule that puts `loading="lazy"` on every `` the site renders. In the next release the home page's LCP goes from 2.1 s to 3.4 s, and nothing else changed. What happened?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 4; Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 7.

choices.text: The cover at the top, the page's LCP element, became a request that waits for the layout
choices.why: A lazy image is only requested once the browser has laid out the page and seen it near the window. For the picture at the top, a request that would have started at once now starts late, and the largest paint waits for it.

choices.text: Lazy images get a low priority, and a low-priority download runs more slowly once it starts
choices.why: Lazy loading decides whether and when the request is made, not how fast the file comes down. The time was lost before the request began.

choices.text: On the first scroll the browser fetched every lazy image at once, and they crowded out the cover
choices.why: Lazy images further down are fetched as the reader approaches each one, in the HTML course's run about 1400 pixels early, not all together. And the LCP was decided before anybody scrolled.

choices.text: A lazy image is never an LCP candidate, so the metric moved to a slower block of text lower down
choices.why: A lazy image can still be the largest thing painted; nothing takes it out of the running. The cover stayed the LCP element and was painted later.

prompt: With every request made 300 ms slower, as on a phone far from the server, a client-rendered page painted its content at 948 ms and the same page rendered on the server at 640 ms. A manager proposes buying more bandwidth from the CDN instead of changing how the page is rendered. Why would that not close the gap?
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 1; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 3.

choices.text: The server-rendered page made fewer requests, and a bigger pipe cannot cut how many files a page needs
choices.why: Both versions made the same four requests. The difference was that the client-rendered one could not start each request until the one before had come back.

choices.text: Bandwidth starts to count above about a megabyte, and both pages are a few kilobytes each
choices.why: There is no such threshold: bandwidth shortens the transfer of any file. These transfers were already tiny, so there was little for it to shorten.

choices.text: The 300 ms is the server's rendering time, which no change to the network or the CDN can make any shorter
choices.why: The server took about two milliseconds before its first byte. The 300 is latency, time before the first byte arrives, added to every request.

choices.text: The gap is one more round trip in a chain, the data after the script, and bandwidth shortens no wait
choices.why: The client-rendered page needed the HTML, then the script, then the data, each found only when the one before had arrived: about three waits of 300 against two. Bandwidth shortens the transfer; latency lengthens everything else.

prompt: A page has no `<main>`. The HTML course's `probe axe` reports `landmark-one-main` for it, yet the team's pipeline test, which runs axe with the tags `wcag2a`, `wcag2aa`, `wcag21a`, `wcag21aa` and `wcag22aa` and expects an empty list, passes. Why?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 2; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 10.

choices.text: The test waits for the `<h1>` before running axe, and by then a script has added the landmark
choices.why: Waiting for the heading makes axe see the page drawn; it adds nothing to it. If no element is a `main`, none appears.

choices.text: That rule is tagged `best-practice`, which those five tags leave out, so it never fails the test
choices.why: axe keeps advice that no WCAG criterion requires, such as one `main` landmark per page, under `best-practice`. The test chose rules by WCAG tag so that a red run always means a criterion failed. The advice is still worth reading.

choices.text: Playwright's Chromium builds an accessibility tree without landmarks, so axe has none to count
choices.why: axe reads the same tree in any Chromium. The course's tests find headings and buttons by role in it, and landmarks are roles too.

choices.text: A missing `<main>` is the HTML validator's job; axe checks contrast, names and alternative text
choices.why: axe has rules about structure as well: `landmark-one-main`, `region` and `page-has-heading-one` were all reported for the soup page in the HTML course.

prompt: In an app built with a meta-framework, the team marks the `/settings` route as left to the browser and the `/orders` route as rendered on each request. Neither is built ahead of time. What does the first response for each one carry?
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 2.

choices.text: Both carry the finished page; they differ only in whether it is kept for the next visitor
choices.why: Being kept or not is the difference between rendering per request and building ahead. A route left to the browser is not rendered on the server at all.

choices.text: `/settings` carries an empty shell for the script to fill; `/orders` carries the finished page
choices.why: Neither is prerendered, and they sit at the two ends of lesson 1's table: the route left to the browser sends the empty container and a script, the per-request route the HTML the server has just drawn.

choices.text: `/settings` carries the finished page and no script; `/orders` the page and a runtime to hydrate it
choices.why: Leaving a route to the browser means the opposite: the server sends no content for it, and all of it is drawn by the script.

choices.text: Both carry an empty shell, since only a prerendered route has content in its first response
choices.why: A route rendered on each request sends the finished page too. What it lacks next to a prerendered one is only the moment the HTML was made.

prompt:
A component test written with Testing Library fails on `getByRole("button", { name: "Reserve" })`. The markup is `
Reserve
`, and clicking it with a mouse works. Which fix serves both the test and the people it stands for?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 2; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 3.

choices.text: Add `data-testid="reserve"` and query with `getByTestId`, which leaves the markup as it is
choices.why: A test id is the last query on the library's list, an escape hatch. Nobody sees it, so a test that needs one is testing a control a screen reader user cannot find either.

choices.text: Query with `getByText("Reserve")` instead, which finds the element by the words on it
choices.why: The test would pass and the defect would stay: the `<div>` is still text in the accessibility tree, and Tab still never reaches it.

choices.text: Give it `cursor: pointer` and a `:focus` style, so it looks and behaves like a control
choices.why: Styles change how it looks. The tree still calls it text and Tab still skips it, because a `<div>` takes no focus.

choices.text: Replace the `<div>` with a `<button type="button">` that calls the same function
choices.why: A `<button>` is announced as a button named by its text, takes the focus and answers Enter and Space. `getByRole` asks the same tree a screen reader reads, so the test passes because the page changed.

prompt: A server-rendered course page takes two seconds to hydrate on a slow phone. It has a *Mark done* `<button type="button">`, whose behaviour is a listener the script attaches, and an *Add session* `<form method="post" action="/sessions">`, whose submit the script also takes over once it runs, and the server handles that address. Somebody uses both a second after the page appears. What happens?
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 4; HTML and CSS, lesson 3.

choices.text: The browser itself sends the form to `/sessions`, and the click on *Mark done* is lost
choices.why: A form with a real `action` is the oldest version of replaying events: the browser builds and sends the request with no script. The button has no fallback, so its click reaches an element with no listener and is forgotten.

choices.text: The browser queues both, and the script handles them once hydration has finished
choices.why: Plain HTML queues nothing. Replaying clicks needs event replay, a small script inline in the page that records them for hydration, and this page has none.

choices.text: Neither does anything, since no element works until the script has attached its listeners
choices.why: That is true of the button. Sending a form is built into HTML: the browser posts it to its `action` with no script at all, as every form in the HTML course did.

choices.text: The button works, since a `<button>` is native, and the form waits for its submit handler
choices.why: A `<button type="button">` does nothing on its own; it is there for a script to give it a job. It is the form that has native behaviour.

prompt: A row of links puts *Order this book* first on screen with `order: -1`. It is last in the HTML, and Tab reaches it last. A colleague proposes `tabindex="1"` on it, so the focus goes there first. What does that do?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 8; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 11.

choices.text: It moves the link to the front of the row's own tab order and leaves the rest of the page alone
choices.why: A positive `tabindex` is not local to the row. It builds a second tab order that runs before everything else on the page.

choices.text: Nothing, because a link is already focusable and `tabindex` only matters for what is not
choices.why: `tabindex` acts on links too: `-1` takes one out of the order, and a positive value puts it before every element that has none.

choices.text: The page's first Tab lands on that link wherever it sits, and the next one goes back to the top
choices.why: A positive value runs a tab order of its own before the document's. The fix is in the HTML: put the link first if it should come first, and lay it out from there.

choices.text: It fixes the focus order and leaves the screen reader's order wrong, a separate criterion
choices.why: It does not fix the focus order either: the focus leaps to the link from wherever it starts. And the reading order stays the HTML's, so both 2.4.3 and 1.3.2 are still at stake.

prompt: The `web-vitals` library reports a click as `INP 1888 ms poor  (input 1, processing 1762, presentation 125)`. Where should the work start?
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 5.

choices.text: With whatever kept the main thread busy before the click, such as hydrating, since input delay comes first
choices.why: The input delay was 1 millisecond. Nothing was in the way when the click arrived.

choices.text: With the stylesheet: presentation is style and layout, and a smaller stylesheet lays out faster
choices.why: Presentation is 125 of the 1888 milliseconds. Removing all of it would still leave the interaction poor.

choices.text: With the server's response time, since the click was waiting for data the page fetched
choices.why: INP ends at the next paint after the interaction, and its three parts have no network in them. A handler that showed something at once and fetched afterwards would have a short INP.

choices.text: With the click's own handler, which ran for almost the whole interaction while nothing could be painted
choices.why: Processing was 1762 of the 1888 milliseconds. In lesson 5 the handler counted every course's sessions by filtering all of them for each course; counting once and drawing a hundred items brought the same click to 88 ms.

prompt: Two stylesheets honour reduced motion in different ways. One writes the animation on `.notice` and adds `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .notice { animation: none; } }`. The other writes the animation only inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) { … }`. Why does the accessibility course call the second the safer way round?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 11; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 13.

choices.text: `reduce` is only reported by macOS and iOS, while every system reports `no-preference`
choices.why: Every major system has the setting, *Reduce motion*, *Animation effects*, *Remove animations*, and the browser passes it on as the same media query.

choices.text: A browser that does not know the query matches neither block, and with the second it shows nothing moving
choices.why: With the first, that browser runs the animation, because the block that would remove it never matches. With the second, the animation exists only where the browser said outright that nobody asked for less.

choices.text: `animation: none` does not reach an animation set with the shorthand, only one set with `animation-name`
choices.why: `animation: none` resets the whole shorthand; the HTML course's capture showed `animation-name: none` with the setting on.

choices.text: The second also stops the page's transitions, which `animation: none` leaves running
choices.why: Neither block touches transitions; each speaks only of the animation it names. A transition would need its own rule in either style.

prompt: During a Lighthouse load, three tasks run on the main thread between the first paint and the moment the page settles: one of 120 ms, one of 40 ms and one of 90 ms. Counting them as Total Blocking Time does, how many milliseconds of blocking time is that?
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 6.

prompt: A menu slides in from the left as the page loads, animated on `left` from `-300px` to `0`. It is smooth on the developer's laptop and stutters on a mid-range phone while the page's script is still running. Why does moving it with `transform: translateX()` instead help?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 12; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 10.

choices.text: Each frame is then only compositing, with no layout or paint on the busy main thread
choices.why: Animating `left` lays out and paints every frame, and a frame has about 16 milliseconds, which one layout on a phone can spend. A transform only changes compositing: the HTML course counted 0 layouts in a second for it, against 62 for a margin.

choices.text: A transform moves the menu by whole pixels, so fewer pixels are repainted than with `left`
choices.why: What differs is not how many pixels change but which stages run. `left` changes geometry, and geometry means layout and then paint.

choices.text: Phones hold an animation on `left` to 30 frames a second, and a transform runs at the screen's rate
choices.why: The browser tries to run both on every frame; the HTML course counted 62 layouts in a second for a margin. They stutter because each of those frames costs a layout.

choices.text: `left` needs `position: absolute`, which puts the menu on a layer and repaints the page under it
choices.why: `left` also applies to relative, fixed and sticky boxes, and positioning alone does not promote a layer. The cost is the layout each new value of `left` asks for.

prompt: Match each response to the `Cache-Control` that lesson 9 gives it.
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 9; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

pairs.left: `/assets/index-B_kobX3K.js`, named after a hash of its contents
a page showing one signed-in student's own sessions
a page showing somebody's payment details
a course page that is the same for everybody, which a CDN may answer for ten seconds without asking

prompt: A hero is `width: 100vw`, and on Windows the page scrolls a few pixels sideways. Someone fixes it by wrapping the whole page in `<div class="wrapper">` with `overflow: hidden`. The next bug report says the months' `position: sticky; top: 0` headings no longer stick. What would have fixed the first problem without causing the second?
hint: HTML and CSS, lessons 6 and 7.

choices.text: `overflow: auto` on the wrapper, which hides the sideways scroll only when there is something to scroll
choices.why: `auto` makes the wrapper a scrolling ancestor exactly as `hidden` does, and the headings would stick to a box that never moves.

choices.text: `top: 0` written on the wrapper as well, so the headings measure their inset from the page
choices.why: An inset on a static wrapper does nothing, and the headings already have theirs. What broke is which ancestor they stick to.

choices.text: `position: relative` on the wrapper, so the headings have a positioned ancestor to stick within
choices.why: Sticky does not look for a positioned ancestor; that is the rule for `absolute`. It sticks within the nearest scrolling ancestor, which `overflow: hidden` made the wrapper.

choices.text: `width: 100%` on the hero, since `100vw` counts the vertical scrollbar and the page does not
choices.why: With classic scrollbars, `100vw` includes the scrollbar's width, so the hero is wider than the page. `100%` is the page's width, nothing scrolls sideways, and no ancestor needs an `overflow`.

prompt: A site's service worker answers everything under `/assets/` cache first. A teammate changes the build so the files there are called `app.js` and `app.css`, with no hash, "so the addresses stay stable". The next deploy changes `app.js` and leaves `sw.js` as it was. What do returning visitors run?
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 10; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: The new `app.js`, since the page is network first and names the script just deployed
choices.why: The page does name `/assets/app.js`, and that address is in the worker's cache. Cache first answers it from the copy without asking the network.

choices.text: The old `app.js`, from the worker's cache, until a new worker version replaces that cache
choices.why: Cache first is right only for a file that never changes at its address, which a hashed name guarantees. With a fixed name the new build lives at the same address, and the copy wins. A new name is the only correction a cache cannot miss.

choices.text: The new `app.js`, because the browser checks for updates on every navigation and sees the change
choices.why: What the browser checks on a navigation is `/sw.js` itself, and that file did not change. No new worker installs, and the old one keeps answering from its cache.

choices.text: Whichever comes back first, since cache first races the copy against the network
choices.why: Racing the two is not what cache first does: it returns the copy if there is one, and asks the network only when there is not.

prompt: A stylesheet sets no font size on `<html>`, and a heading has `font-size: 1.5rem`. A reader with low vision has set their browser's default text size to 20 pixels. How many pixels is the heading's font size for them?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 6.

prompt: The planner's text is set in IBM Plex Sans with `font-display: swap`, and on a slow phone the swap moves a line of the course list. Which changes reduce that shift without making the text wait for the font? Choose all that apply.
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 7.

choices.text: Preload the two WOFF2 files with `as="font"` and `crossorigin`
choices.why: The fonts then start with the stylesheet instead of a step after it, and on the lesson's slowed run the text was painted once, in Plex.

choices.text: Switch to `font-display: block`, so the text is drawn only once the font is there
choices.why: There is then nothing to swap, and the text is invisible until the font arrives: the lesson's LCP waited for it, about three hundred milliseconds later than with `swap`.

choices.text: Add an `@font-face` for `local("Arial")` with the `size-adjust` measured against Plex, listed after it
choices.why: The fallback then takes the room Plex will take, so when the swap comes the letters change and the lines stay where they were.

choices.text: Put `system-ui` between the web font and `sans-serif`, so the fallback is the system's own interface font
choices.why: `system-ui` is a different shape on every system, the opposite of a fallback chosen to match. The lesson took it out of the list.

choices.text: Name Arial in the font stack rather than leaving the fallback to `sans-serif` alone
choices.why: Arial measured within one per cent of Plex's width. `sans-serif` alone gets whatever the system likes, such as DejaVu Sans, about an eighth wider.

choices.text: Drop `crossorigin` from the preload, since the font comes from the page's own server
choices.why: Fonts are always requested in CORS mode. A preload without it does not match the real request, and the font is fetched a second time.

prompt: A grid container 800 pixels wide has `grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 3fr` and `gap: 16px`. How many pixels wide is its third column?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 9.

prompt: On a phone 390 pixels wide, a page lays itself out 980 wide and its 32-pixel heading comes out about 13 on the glass. Complete the line its head is missing: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=___, initial-scale=1">`
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 1.

prompt: Only the stats page draws a chart, and the chart library is most of the bundle. Complete the line that fetches the chart's code the first time it runs, and that makes Vite give that code a chunk of its own: `(await ___("./chart.ts")).showChart(p)`
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 8.

prompt: A site moves to Tailwind and keeps its old `site.css`, which is in no cascade layer and contains `a { color: #8a1c1c; }`. A link written `<a class="text-white bg-green-700" href="…">` shows red text. `.text-white` is (0,1,0) and `a` is (0,0,1). Why does the red win?
hint: HTML and CSS, lessons 10 and 13.

choices.text: Tailwind's utilities are in a layer, and styles in no layer beat every layer before specificity is asked
choices.why: Between layers the order decides first, and unlayered styles rank above all of them, so specificity is never compared. Importing the old file into a low layer, with `@import … layer(…)`, lets the utilities win again.

choices.text: `site.css` is linked after Tailwind's file, and the later of two rules wins whatever their specificity
choices.why: Order only decides between rules of equal specificity in the same layer. Here the two never reach specificity, because one is in a layer and the other is not.

choices.text: Preflight resets links with a higher specificity than the utilities, and `site.css` builds on that
choices.why: Preflight sits in `base`, below `utilities`, and it sets links to the colour of the text around them. Nothing builds on a reset.

choices.text: A colour set on `a` itself beats one that reaches it through a class, as the link blue beats a parent's colour
choices.why: `text-white` does not reach the link by inheritance; it is a rule that matches the link itself. A matched rule beating an inherited value is true and is not what happened here.

prompt: The planner, once installed, should open in a window of its own with no address bar and none of the browser's toolbar. Complete the member of its web app manifest: `"display": "___"`
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 11.

prompt: A booking page has `<form action="/cancel" method="get">` with a hidden field for the booking and a *Cancel my reservation* button. The site sits behind a CDN. Besides the address bar showing `/cancel?booking=…`, what goes wrong with GET here?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 3; Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 9.

choices.text: A hidden field is left out of a GET request, so the server cannot tell which booking to cancel
choices.why: A GET sends every field that has a name, hidden ones included, in the query string. The booking would be right there in the address.

choices.text: Native validation is skipped for a GET form, so an empty booking reaches the server unchecked
choices.why: The browser validates before sending with either method; `method` only decides where the data travels.

choices.text: A cache's copy answers the request, the server never hears of it, and the booking stands
choices.why: GET is for requests that only read, and caches act on that: in practice only `GET` and `HEAD` are kept. A GET that changes something can be answered from a copy, bookmarked, or sent again with the back button.

choices.text: A CDN will not forward a GET that has a query string, so the request stops at the edge
choices.why: CDNs forward query strings constantly; a search is a GET with one. The danger runs the other way: a copy served instead of the request being forwarded.

prompt: A shop regenerates each page incrementally, with an age of an hour. A product is renamed. For a while the product's own page shows the new name and the category page that lists it still shows the old one. What makes both pages change together?
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 3.

choices.text: A shorter age on the category page, so it regenerates as soon as the product page does
choices.why: Each page still regenerates on its own, when it is asked for after its age. A shorter age shortens the disagreement and cannot line the two up.

choices.text: Sending both pages with `stale-while-revalidate`, so the old copies are refreshed in the background
choices.why: That is the same rule as the age, applied by a CDN: each copy is refreshed on its own request, so the two still change at different moments.

choices.text: On-demand revalidation, with every page rendered from that data tagged and marked at once
choices.why: A timer regenerates a page because time passed, one page at a time. Marking every copy rendered from the same data, as the lesson did with one tag for the home page and the course pages, regenerates them together.

choices.text: Keeping both copies on the same server, since copies on two servers go stale at different moments
choices.why: That is a different disagreement, between two servers' copies of the same page. On one server, two different pages still regenerate separately.

prompt: Put a service worker's life in order, from the page that installs it to the requests it answers.
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 10.
items: A page calls `navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js")`, and the browser downloads the file
`install` runs once, the moment to fetch what the worker wants to have from the start
`activate` runs once nothing older controls a page, the moment to delete what an older version left
Each request from a page it controls arrives as a `fetch` event, and the script decides the answer
trap: The usual slip is to have the worker answer requests straight after registering. It installs first, activates only once no older version controls a page, and controls the pages opened after that, so `fetch` comes last.

prompt: A heading is brown in the stylesheet and grey on the page. Put the HTML course's procedure for finding out why in order.
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 5.
items: Right-click the heading and choose Inspect
Read the Styles pane, which lists every rule that matched, the most important first
Find the `color` declarations and the one that is not struck through
Read that rule's file and line, and whether it won on specificity or on order
trap: The tempting shortcut is to add `!important` to your own rule before reading the list. In the course's case the winner was a forgotten duplicate lower in the file, and the list shows that in a minute.

prompt: Every field of an order form holds a value that breaks its rule. Match each field to the flag `validity` reports for it.
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 3.

prompt: A page's axe run, with every WCAG 2.2 AA tag, reports no violations. Which of these could still be wrong with it? Choose all that apply.
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 2; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 10.

choices.text: Two links called *Click here* that go to different pages
choices.why: *Click here* is a name, and axe accepts it. Whether a link's text says where it goes is a question of meaning, not of the document's structure.

choices.text: A book cover inside a link, with no `alt` attribute at all
choices.why: That is exactly what axe finds: `image-alt` for the picture, and `link-name` for the link it leaves with no name.

choices.text: A logo whose `alt` is `image`
choices.why: `alt="image"` passes every rule. Whether the text says what the picture means is for a person to judge.

choices.text: Done sessions drawn in `#aaaaaa` on white, at 2.32:1
choices.why: A contrast ratio can be decided from the document. axe reported this one as `color-contrast`, against the 4.5:1 that AA asks of text that size.

choices.text: A focus outline removed by a style, with nothing put in its place
choices.why: A style that removes the outline is valid CSS, and axe does not press Tab to see where the focus went. Whether the focused element is visible is lesson 11's question.

choices.text: A text field that no label, attribute or text names at all
choices.why: A field with no name is one of the things axe can decide, as it can decide a button with no name or a duplicate id.

prompt: A script inserts a consent banner at the top of `<body>` a second after the page has painted, with no tap or click from the reader, and the page's CLS goes over 0.1. Which way of showing it keeps the shift out of the score?
hint: HTML and CSS, lesson 7; Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 5.

choices.text: Insert it on the reader's first scroll, since a shift right after the reader acts is excused
choices.why: The excuse covers an interaction, a click, a tap or a key, and the half second after it. Scrolling is not one, and the reader did not ask for a banner.

choices.text: `position: fixed` at the bottom of the window, so it covers part of the screen and moves no other box
choices.why: A fixed box is out of the flow, so its arrival moves nothing, which is how the planner's install button appears late without a shift. It costs screen space for as long as it stays, and must not cover the element that has the focus.

choices.text: Fade it in from `opacity: 0`, which the compositor animates without a layout
choices.why: The fade is cheap, but the box takes its room in the flow the moment it is inserted, and everything under it moves down.

choices.text: Give the banner `z-index: 9999`, so it is drawn over the page instead of pushing it down
choices.why: `z-index` decides what is drawn in front where boxes overlap. A box in the normal flow still takes its room and pushes what follows it.

prompt: Which of these, in a page's `<head>`, hold back its first paint? Choose all that apply.
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 7; HTML and CSS, lesson 1.

choices.text: `<script type="module" src="/assets/index.js"></script>`, as Vite writes it
choices.why: A module is fetched without stopping the parser and runs once the document has been read, as with `defer`.

choices.text: `<link rel="stylesheet" href="site.css">`
choices.why: The browser waits for every stylesheet in the head before it paints, because drawing the page unstyled and then again would make it jump.

choices.text: `<script src="menu.js" defer></script>`
choices.why: `defer` fetches it while the parser carries on and runs it afterwards, so the HTML is read at full speed.

choices.text: `<script src="menu.js"></script>`
choices.why: With none of `defer`, `async` or `type="module"`, the browser stops reading the HTML until the script has been fetched and run, because it may write into the page.

choices.text: `<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/plex-400.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>`
choices.why: A preload starts a download early and blocks nothing. What it costs is bandwidth taken from other requests.

prompt: A home page's LCP is 3.8 s on phones. The `web-vitals` attribution splits it into time to first byte 0.3 s, resource load delay 2.4 s, resource load duration 0.6 s and element render delay 0.5 s. The LCP element is a hero picture that a carousel script inserts. What is the first fix?
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lessons 5 and 7.

choices.text: Compress the picture to AVIF and offer smaller files in `srcset`, since it is the LCP element
choices.why: That shortens the resource load duration, 0.6 of the 3.8 seconds. The largest part is the wait before the download even began.

choices.text: Inline the critical CSS, so nothing holds back the paint once the picture has arrived
choices.why: That works on the element render delay, 0.5 seconds here. Worth doing later, and not where most of the time went.

choices.text: Serve the HTML from a CDN close to the visitor, which brings every later part forward
choices.why: That shortens the time to first byte, already 0.3 seconds, and moves the other parts only by what it saves.

choices.text: Put the picture's `` in the HTML the server sends, so the browser finds it without the script
choices.why: Resource load delay is the time until the image began to load: 2.4 of the 3.8 seconds, spent waiting for a script to name it. In the first response, with `fetchpriority="high"`, the request starts at once.

prompt: A redesign moves a product photo from the full width into a column half the window wide on desktops, and the CSS is updated. The `` keeps `srcset="p-480.jpg 480w, p-960.jpg 960w, p-1600.jpg 1600w"` and has no `sizes`. On a 1280-pixel window at a pixel ratio of 1, the LCP got slower. Why?
hint: Rendering, Performance and PWA, lesson 5; HTML and CSS, lesson 4.

choices.text: With no `sizes` the browser assumes `100vw`, so it fetches a file for 1280 pixels to draw one 640 wide
choices.why: `sizes` is a promise about the layout that nothing checks, read before the page is laid out. Left out, it is the whole window, so Chromium takes the 1600 where the 960 would do, and the LCP's resource load duration grows with it.

choices.text: With no `sizes` the browser ignores `srcset` and falls back to `src`, which is the largest file
choices.why: `srcset` is still read. A missing `sizes` only changes how wide the browser believes the image will be drawn, which becomes the full window.

choices.text: The browser reads the new CSS width before it chooses, and a half-width column calls for a sharper file
choices.why: The browser chooses the file before it has worked out the layout, which is why `sizes` repeats what the CSS says. It never saw the half width.

choices.text: A narrower column has fewer pixels, and Chromium then takes the widest file so the photo is not soft
choices.why: Chromium took the narrowest file at least as wide as the drawn width times the pixel ratio. A narrower drawing would mean a smaller file, had `sizes` said so.

prompt:
In `view.ts` a colleague draws the **Done** control as `
Done
` with a click listener. The component test `getByRole("button", { name: "Done" })` now throws, and the colleague proposes changing the test. What should change instead?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 3; HTML and CSS, lesson 2.

choices.text: The test: `getByText("Done")` finds it, and the words on it are what a person reads anyway
choices.why: It finds the words and hides the defect. The `<div>` is still text to a screen reader and is never reached by Tab, and the test has stopped saying so.

choices.text: The test: `findByRole` waits, and the listener is attached only after the element is drawn
choices.why: Nothing here arrives late. `findByRole` waits for an element that will appear, and no amount of waiting turns a `<div>` into a button.

choices.text: The markup: a `<button>`, because the `<div>` is plain text in the accessibility tree
choices.why: `getByRole` asks the accessibility tree, where the `<div>` is text with no role. The failing test is reporting what a keyboard and a screen reader meet, and `<button>` brings the role, the focus and both keys.

choices.text: The test: a `data-testid` on the `<div>` survives any rename of its class
choices.why: A test id is the last resort, and a person never sees one. A test that needs it is finding something no person can find either.

prompt: The planner's API allows two origins, `http://localhost:5173` and `http://localhost:4173`, and sits behind a shared cache. Somebody deletes `vary: "Origin"` from `corsHeaders`, calling it a detail about caches. What can go wrong now?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 7; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: The cache files one answer per address, so 4173 is handed the copy whose allow header names 5173
choices.why: A cache keys an answer by the address unless `Vary` says another header decided it. Served the copy made for 5173, the browser on 4173 compares the origins and refuses to let the page read it.

choices.text: Without `Vary`, the browser reads the allow header as a `*`, and any site may read the answers
choices.why: No browser reads a missing `Vary` as a wildcard. The allow header still names one origin, and with credentials a `*` would be refused anyway.

choices.text: The preflight is no longer remembered for `600` seconds, so each request costs one more `OPTIONS`
choices.why: That memory is `access-control-max-age`, answered on the `OPTIONS` itself, and removing `Vary` leaves it as it was.

choices.text: The browser attaches cookies only to answers that vary on `Origin`, so `credentials: "include"` breaks
choices.why: Whether a cross-origin `fetch` sends cookies depends on `credentials` and on `Allow-Credentials: true`, not on `Vary`.

prompt: A tutorial keeps the planner's JWT in `localStorage` and sends it in an `Authorization` header. A colleague defends it: web storage belongs to one origin, so no other site can read it. What does that defence miss?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 5; JavaScript, lesson 18.

choices.text: Storage is shared by every port of a host, so a page on `localhost:3000` reads what `localhost:5173` wrote
choices.why: The port is part of the origin, so those two are different origins and cannot read each other's storage.

choices.text: `localStorage` is emptied when the tab is closed, so people are signed out at random
choices.why: That is `sessionStorage`. `localStorage` keeps a value until somebody deletes it, which makes it worse for a secret, not better.

choices.text: A token in an `Authorization` header is sent by the browser to every site on its own, which is CSRF
choices.why: The page's own code adds that header. The browser attaches a cookie on its own; it never attaches a header the code did not write.

choices.text: The threat is a script inside the page, which shares the origin; `HttpOnly` keeps a cookie from it
choices.why: The origin boundary keeps out other sites, and an injected script or a library is not another site. A token the page holds is as safe as the page is free of scripts; an `HttpOnly` cookie is unreadable by all of them.

prompt: `expect(await page.getByRole("listitem").count()).toBe(3)` passes on Ana's laptop and fails on some CI runs with `Received: 0`. The check is required, so her pull request cannot merge. What is the fix?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 4; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 3.

choices.text: `await page.waitForTimeout(1000)` before the count, so a slow runner has time to fetch the data
choices.why: A fixed pause is too long on a fast machine and too short on a slow one, so the test stays flaky, only less often.

choices.text: A web-first `toHaveCount(3)` on the locator, which keeps asking the page until the list is drawn
choices.why: The original reads the page once, at `load`, before the data arrives. A web-first assertion retries until the answer is right or its timeout passes, and waits exactly as long as the network needs.

choices.text: Re-run the job until it is green: the code did not change, so one green run proves it works
choices.why: A green run of a flaky test proves the machine was fast that time. The same code fails again on a busy afternoon.

choices.text: Have an administrator merge past the rule, since the failure belongs to the runner and not the code
choices.why: An administrator's bypass is one of the ways red code reaches `main`, and here the fault is in the test's own timing, which a bypass leaves in place.

prompt: A repository's ruleset requires `CI / check`. In a tidy-up the job is renamed `test`. A month later `main` holds a commit whose own run of `e2e/a11y.spec.ts` was red with `color-contrast: 2`. What is the likeliest way it got in?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 10; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 3.

choices.text: The rule waited for a `CI / check` that never ran again, and whoever took it off left nothing required
choices.why: A renamed job leaves the rule waiting for a check that no longer exists, every merge stalls, and the usual way out is removing the requirement. From then on red is a suggestion.

choices.text: `color-contrast` is one of axe's `best-practice` rules, so a red result from it never blocks a merge
choices.why: `color-contrast` tests 1.4.3, a level AA criterion, and the test selects rules by the WCAG tags. Its red is a criterion failing.

choices.text: A required check that no job reports counts as passed, so the rename opened the gate at once
choices.why: It is the other way round: a required check that never reports keeps the merge button grey, which is why somebody ends up removing it.

choices.text: Rulesets govern direct pushes to `main`, and a merge made with the button skips them
choices.why: The rule is precisely about merges: it keeps the button grey until the named check is green on the latest commit.

prompt:
Bruno's pull request draws each session's note with `note.innerHTML = s.note.replace(/\n/g, "
")`. Reviewing it, which comment does Ana post on that line?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 13; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 9.

choices.text: **nit:** I'd use `textContent` here, but `innerHTML` works too, so take it or leave it as you like
choices.why: A nit is a point the author is free to ignore, and this one is not: a note somebody typed becomes markup in the page.

choices.text: **question:** is `innerHTML` the right call for the note? I might have written it another way myself
choices.why: Ana knows the answer, so a question makes Bruno guess how much she cares. When you are sure, say so.

choices.text: **blocking:** a note holding `<b>` becomes an element; `textContent` with `pre-line` keeps the breaks
choices.why: It says what happens, why it matters and a fix, aimed at the line. `innerHTML` is a sink: it parses the person's text as markup, which is cross-site scripting, and must change before the merge.

choices.text: You forgot to escape the note. This is wrong and should never have been opened in this state
choices.why: It is aimed at Bruno, not the code, and it says neither what happens nor how to fix it.

prompt: A teammate adds `<button onclick="toggleTheme()">Theme</button>` to `index.html`. It works under `npm run dev`. On the built site, served with the planner's policy, pressing it does nothing and the console names `script-src 'self'`. What is the fix?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 8; JavaScript, lesson 12.

choices.text: Add `'unsafe-inline'` to `script-src`, a keyword that only lets handler attributes run
choices.why: `'unsafe-inline'` lets every inline script run, injected ones included, which undoes the line that earns the policy its place.

choices.text: Send the same headers from the dev server too, so the button fails while developing
choices.why: That breaks the dev server, whose CSS arrives as inline `<style>` elements the policy refuses, and the button stays broken.

choices.text: Load `toggleTheme` from a CDN with an `integrity` hash, which the policy then trusts as its own
choices.why: `script-src 'self'` allows scripts from the page's own origin and nowhere else. Integrity checks a file; it does not widen the list.

choices.text: Bind it with `addEventListener` in the planner's module: an `onclick` attribute is inline code
choices.why: An `onclick` attribute is code in a string inside the markup, and the policy refuses inline code. A listener added from the bundled script comes from the origin, so it runs.

prompt: The planner's weekly total pulses. A colleague would keep `.week { animation: pulse 1s ease-in-out 3; }` and add the global rule from `html-css`: a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block that cuts every animation to `0.01ms`. Lesson 13 moves the animation inside `no-preference` instead. What does that buy?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 13; HTML and CSS, lesson 12.

choices.text: With `no-preference`, readers who asked for less motion get a short fade in place of the pulse
choices.why: A fade for those readers is an option a site may choose to write. Moving the animation into `no-preference` gives them nothing at all.

choices.text: A browser that does not know the query matches neither block, and so shows no pulse at all
choices.why: With the animation inside `no-preference`, the default is stillness and only a browser that passes the setting on as no preference moves. The reduce block gives the pulse to everybody whose browser does not pass the setting on.

choices.text: A `0.01ms` animation is below what axe accepts, so the colleague's version fails `e2e/a11y.spec.ts`
choices.why: axe reads the document and never times an animation. Motion is one of the questions lesson 10 leaves to other tests.

choices.text: A `reduce` block is ignored when the rule it overrides comes earlier in the stylesheet
choices.why: Later rules win in the cascade, which is why the global rule is loaded after the others. Order is not what separates the two approaches.

prompt: After the planner gets a dark theme, `e2e/palette.spec.ts` reports `--link: 3.02:1` in the dark scheme only. Where does the fix belong?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 13; HTML and CSS, lesson 10.

choices.text: A new `--link` in the dark block only; the focus ring is drawn in it too, so it follows
choices.why: The dark block redefines the custom properties on `:root`, and it left the green as it was. Redefining `--link` there fixes the links on dark only, and `:focus-visible`, drawn in `var(--link)`, changes with them.

choices.text: Nowhere: link colour is 1.4.11 non-text contrast, whose bar is 3:1, and 3.02:1 clears it
choices.why: A link is text, so 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1. 3:1 is the bar for a control's parts and a focus ring, not for words.

choices.text: `color-scheme: light dark` on `:root`, which makes the browser lighten the page's links in dark
choices.why: That declaration lets the browser draw its own parts, buttons, fields and scroll bars, in either scheme. The planner already has it, and it does not recolour the page's links.

choices.text: A fixed colour on `a { color: … }`, since a property redefined inside `@media` is read only once
choices.why: Redefining custom properties inside a media query is exactly how the theme works, and a fixed colour would be wrong in the light scheme.

prompt:
To announce a new session, a colleague adds `

Session added: …

` inside `render`, which begins with `root.replaceChildren()`. The Playwright check of the status text passes, and NVDA says nothing. Why?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 12.

choices.text: A status waits until the reader has finished, so a message after a button press has to be `role="alert"`
choices.why: `alert` interrupts, and belongs to errors that cannot wait. A polite status is read; this one is silent for another reason.

choices.text: A paragraph cannot hold a live region; a reader watches a `<div>` with `aria-live`
choices.why: `role="status"` on any element makes it a live region, and the lesson's fix is a paragraph.

choices.text: It is born full and remade on every draw, and a reader only announces changes to a region already there
choices.why: A reader watches the live regions in the page and reads what changes in them. One born full is usually read by nobody, so the region is made once beside the root and its text set afterwards.

choices.text: A reader reads out only what takes the focus, so the focus has to be moved onto the message itself
choices.why: A live region is exactly the way to be heard without the focus. The lesson's fix puts the focus back in the form and lets the status speak.

prompt: A CSS change leaves the planner's **Add session** button covered by the weekly total on narrow screens. Which is the lowest layer of tests that can see it?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 1.

choices.text: A component test, since `getByRole` finds only the controls a person can actually reach
choices.why: `getByRole` reads the accessibility tree, and a covered button is still in it with its role and name. jsdom has no layout to say what is on top.

choices.text: The type checker, since `tsc` reads `style.css` together with `view.ts`
choices.why: `tsc` reads TypeScript files and the shapes of values. A stylesheet is outside what it checks.

choices.text: A unit test of `render`, since what `render` returns is the page itself
choices.why: `render` draws into a root and returns nothing, and no layer below the browser computes where anything sits.

choices.text: An end-to-end test in a real Chromium, because jsdom computes no layout and cannot tell covered from free
choices.why: jsdom is the DOM without layout, CSS or a screen, so whether one element covers another exists only in a browser. That is the top of the pyramid, and here it is the lowest layer that can see the fault.

prompt: In planning poker for *Make every page pass axe*, the cards come up 2, 13, 3 and 3. What does the team do next?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 16.

choices.text: Write down 5, the average of the four, so that nobody's estimate is thrown away
choices.why: Averaging hides the reason behind the 13, which is the information nobody else at the table has yet.

choices.text: The 13 and the 2 explain their numbers, then the team votes again
choices.why: The highest and the lowest say why. A 13 is a signal, and its reason is often a problem the others had not seen, found in two minutes rather than in production.

choices.text: Take 3, the number most of the team chose, and move straight on to the next ticket
choices.why: A majority is not an argument. The point of revealing at once is that a quiet person's worry gets the same weight as the others.

choices.text: Record 13, the safest number, so planning is not caught short
choices.why: A 13 is not a size to record. Inflating estimates only makes the team's velocity meaningless.

prompt: To keep a payment provider's secret key out of the history, a colleague writes it into `.env.local` as `VITE_PAYMENT_KEY`, sees that `git status` shows nothing to commit, and reads it with `import.meta.env.VITE_PAYMENT_KEY`. What is wrong?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 2.

choices.text: The build copies any `VITE_` value into the bundle, so every visitor reads a key Git never saw
choices.why: The ignore list keeps the file out of the history, and the prefix puts the value in the JavaScript every visitor downloads. A secret key belongs on a server the team controls.

choices.text: The template commits `.env.local`, so the key is already in the history and has to be revoked
choices.why: The template's `.gitignore` has `*.local`, which is why `git status` showed nothing. The leak is elsewhere.

choices.text: Vite reads only `.env`, so `import.meta.env.VITE_PAYMENT_KEY` comes out `undefined` in the build
choices.why: Vite reads `.env.local` in every mode. The value arrives, and that is the problem.

choices.text: Nothing: the bundle is made on the build machine, and `.gitignore` keeps the key out of every single clone
choices.why: Where the bundle is made does not matter once it is served. Anything in it is readable by everybody who can open the page.

prompt: Ana's push is rejected, and `git pull` stops with `fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches.` She has one commit nobody else has. She runs `git pull --rebase` and pushes. Why does that not break the rule against rebasing shared commits?
