hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 7; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 6.

choices.text: Because `--rebase` makes a merge commit, and a merge rewrites nothing that already exists
choices.why: `--no-rebase` is the one that merges. `--rebase` replays commits, which gives them new ids.

choices.text: Because a pull rebases Bruno's commit onto hers, and the remote accepts what it gets back
choices.why: Bruno's commit is the base and is left exactly as it was. Nothing that came from the remote gets a new id.

choices.text: Because `--ff-only` runs first and joins the branches, leaving the rebase nothing to rewrite
choices.why: `--ff-only` accepts only the case with nothing to join and refuses otherwise. Here the branches had diverged.

choices.text: Because the one commit it rewrites is her own, never pushed, replayed on top of Bruno's commit
choices.why: The rule is about commits somebody else already has. Hers had never left her machine, so it alone gets a new id, and the push moves `main` forward.

prompt: A component test of `view.ts` needs stand-ins. Following lesson 2, which of these should it replace? Choose all that apply.
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 2.

choices.text: the clock that `today()` reads
choices.why: A test cannot control the time, and `vi.useFakeTimers()` with `setSystemTime` lets it say what `new Date()` returns.

choices.text: `weekTotal`, which the view calls to draw the total
choices.why: Mocking it makes the test faster by nothing and blind to the defect the first test found. It is code the test can run for real.

choices.text: the network a fetch would go out on
choices.why: The network is outside what a test controls, so it is one of the three things the lesson names to replace.

choices.text: the `update` callback that `render` hands a new plan to
choices.why: `render`'s output is a call, so the test passes `vi.fn()` and reads the plan it received, which is still asserting on output.

choices.text: `markDone` from `planner.ts`, so the test can check it was called once
choices.why: That asserts on how the code works today, and it fails for a refactoring and passes for a bug. The test reads the plan that came out.

choices.text: the simulated page, so the test does not depend on jsdom
choices.why: jsdom is what lets a component test run at all; it is the environment, not an input to stand in for.

prompt: Before lesson 6's fix, the planner's server set `Set-Cookie: sid=…; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/`. Which of these are true of that cookie? Choose all that apply.
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 6; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: one request to a plain `http://` address would carry it in the clear
choices.why: It has no `Secure`, which is the attribute that keeps a cookie off plain HTTP.

choices.text: a script on the page can copy it out of `document.cookie`
choices.why: `HttpOnly` is there, so `document.cookie` does not show it.

choices.text: with neither `Max-Age` nor `Expires`, the browser keeps it until the window closes
choices.why: That makes it a session cookie in the browser's sense, with no lifetime chosen on purpose.

choices.text: with no `Domain`, the browser sends it to every subdomain of the host
choices.why: Left out, `Domain` keeps the cookie with exactly the host that set it. Writing it is what widens it.

choices.text: its name has no `__Host-` prefix, so the browser enforces none of `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`
choices.why: The prefix turns those three rules into one the browser checks. Without it, a mistake in them is silent.

choices.text: clearing it at sign-out also ends the login on the server
choices.why: Whether the login ends is the server's decision. Lesson 6's test sent the old cookie again after sign-out and got 200.

prompt: A team copies its repository, every branch and every commit, to a new hosting service and sets nothing up there. Which of these no longer happen? Choose all that apply.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 8.

choices.text: a pull request's merge button waiting for one approval
choices.why: Required approvals are a setting of the hosting service on its copy of `main`, and the new service has none.

choices.text: every commit keeping its author, its message and its parent
choices.why: Those are inside each commit. Any copy of the repository carries them.

choices.text: a `git push --force` to `main` being refused
choices.why: That refusal is a protection rule on the server, lesson 7's warning turned into a lock, and it did not travel with the commits.

choices.text: `git status` leaving out what `.gitignore` names
choices.why: `.gitignore` is a file in the repository, read by Git on each machine, so it works in every clone.

choices.text: a merge refused until the checks have passed
choices.why: Required checks are part of the branch's protection, which lives on the old server and not in Git.

choices.text: `git merge --abort` putting a conflicted merge back as it was
choices.why: It is a Git command, run on your own machine, and needs nothing from any server.

prompt: On a planner course page, read from the top, the controls are the back link, one **Done** button, a date field, the Minutes field, the Note field and **Add session**. Starting with nothing focused, how many presses of Tab does it take in Chromium for the focus to land on **Add session**?
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 11.

prompt: The bakery's team of four finishes about 30 points in a normal ten-day sprint. In this one Ana and Bruno have all ten days, Carla has 7 and Diego 8. Scaling the usual 30 by the days available, as lesson 18 does, about how many points is the team's capacity?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 18.

prompt: The planner's page on `http://localhost:5173` calls `fetch` with `method: "POST"` and `content-type: application/json` to the API on port 3000. Before that request leaves, the browser sends one of its own to the same address, using the HTTP method ___, the one that asks a server what is allowed.
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 7; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

prompt: Since the tag `v1.0`, `git log --oneline v1.0..HEAD` shows `fix(view): give the back link a name` and `feat(view): a dark theme`, with no `!` and no `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer. By lesson 11's rule, the next release is tagged ___.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 11.

prompt: axe found icons with no `alt` and a done grey at 2.32:1 in the planner. Put the task in order, from the ticket to the merge.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 12; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 10.
items: Write the ticket, with both pages passing axe at WCAG 2.2 AA as its acceptance criterion
Pull `main`, then start a branch whose name begins with the ticket's number
Add `e2e/a11y.spec.ts` and watch it fail with `image-alt: 3`
Give the icons `alt=""` and the done grey `#6b6b6b`, and watch the test pass
Open the pull request with `Closes #` and the ticket's number in its description
Merge once it is approved and the checks are green
trap: The usual slip is fixing the colours before the test exists. A test written after the fix has never been seen to fail, so nobody knows it can.

prompt: Ana's branch `rolls` changes a price that Bruno also changed on `main`. Put the steps in order, from the rebase to `main` holding her commit.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 6.
items: On `rolls`, run `git rebase main` and read `CONFLICT (content)`
Edit `menu.html` so it says the one price wanted, with the three markers gone
`git add menu.html`, which says this conflict is settled
`git rebase --continue`, and save the message as it is
`git switch main` and `git merge rolls`, which is a fast-forward
trap: The likeliest slip is typing `git commit` after `git add`, as in a merge. During a rebase the step is `git rebase --continue`, so the rebase can go on to the next commit.

prompt: A reviewer is checking the planner for the places text turns into code. Match each line to the safe way lesson 9 gives.
hint: Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 9; JavaScript, lesson 11.

pairs.right: check that `new URL(s).protocol` is `https:` or `http:` first
a function in its place, never a string

prompt: Each situation needs a different way back. Match it to the command lesson 4 gives for it.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4.

pairs.left: an edit to `menu.html`, never added, has to go
a `git add` was a mistake, and the edit should stay in the file
a commit already on the shared `main` took rye bread off by mistake
the last commit, not pushed, has a typo in its message
the last commit, not pushed, should be redone, its change ready to commit again

prompt: A teammate wires a model into the design tool to suggest five names for a new button component, and sets temperature to 0.2 and top-p to 0.5 "to keep it careful". What does lesson 1 say about that setting?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 1.

choices.text: Right for this task: a low temperature and a low top-p together are what lesson 1 sets for anything that ends up in code
choices.why: Lesson 1 gives a low temperature to code, extraction and classification, where there is one correct answer. A list of names is not that, and it also changes one of the two settings, not both.

choices.text: Wrong on both counts: names want variety, near the provider's default, and you change one setting, not both
choices.why: For names, alternatives and test ideas variety is the point, so the temperature stays near the default, often 1. And moving temperature and top-p together leaves nobody able to say which one did what.

choices.text: Harmless: temperature and top-p cancel each other out when both are set, so the reply is drawn exactly as at the defaults
choices.why: They do not cancel. Temperature reshapes the distribution and top-p cuts its tail; set together, both act on the draw.

choices.text: Wrong because names are a task for temperature 0, which makes the model return the same five each time it is asked
choices.why: Temperature 0 gives the same answer every time, which is the opposite of what a request for alternatives wants. Lesson 1 puts names around the provider's default.

prompt: A help widget sends the whole conversation with every new message, as lesson 2's `conversation.py` does. In that capture, all requests up to turn 10 read 6,070 input tokens and all requests up to turn 20 read 24,740. By what factor did doubling the conversation multiply its input tokens? One decimal place.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 2.

prompt: A pull request titled *Compute the subtotal once in total()* was written with an assistant. The diff makes `total()` keep the subtotal in a variable, and all eight tests pass. `discount()` still calls `subtotal()` itself and `shipping()` calls both. Reviewing it in git lesson 13's order, what is the first finding?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 3; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 13.

choices.text: None: eight green tests are what lesson 13's second question, *does it work?*, asks for, so the review can move on to names
choices.why: Green tests say the behaviour did not change. They cannot say whether the change did what was asked, and that is question 1, before *does it work?*.

choices.text: A nit about the variable's name, since a refactoring that keeps the behaviour has nothing left to review except how it reads
choices.why: Names are question 3. A problem in question 1 makes the later questions irrelevant, and this change has one.

choices.text: Question 1 fails: the other two methods still recompute it, so none of the saving the request wanted happens
choices.why: Question 1 is whether the change does what the ticket asked. ai-dev lesson 3 found exactly this: the tests passed and were right to, and the change saved nothing, which only reading the change against the request can find.

choices.text: A blocking comment that the assistant's diff must be rejected outright, because code from an assistant needs a second human author
choices.why: Nothing in either lesson rejects a change for who wrote it. The review answers whether it is good enough to merge, and here the answer comes from what it does.

prompt: A front-end project keeps `VITE_PAYMENTS_SECRET=sk_live_…` in `.env.local`, which `.gitignore` covers. Its author says the key is safe "because git ignores the file and the editor's assistant only reads the repository". Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 3; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 2.

choices.text: An assistant sends whatever is open in a tab, and `.gitignore` says nothing to the editor about that
choices.why: ai-dev lesson 3: an ignored file is still a file on disk, and a tab is a tab. Only an exclusion list the assistant reads keeps it out.

choices.text: The `VITE_` prefix tells the build to copy the value into the bundle that every visitor downloads
choices.why: front-delivery lesson 2: Vite copies a variable in because its name says so. A secret key in the bundle is readable by anybody who opens the page.

choices.text: Minifying the bundle renames the value, so a string copied into it can no longer be read
choices.why: Minifying renames variables. A string stays a string, and `grep` finds it in the built file.

choices.text: If a request carrying the key was refused by the model, the key did not leave and needs no rotating
choices.why: A refusal is a reply, and it comes back after the request has gone with everything in it. A secret that left is rotated.

choices.text: A key that starts with `sk_` is the publishable kind, meant for the browser
choices.why: front-delivery lesson 2 gives `pk_` against `sk_` as the common convention, and `sk_` is the secret one, for a server only.

prompt: An assistant writes a fix for a date input that accepted `31/02`, and a test for it in the same reply. The test passes on its first run. What do ai-dev lesson 5 and the portfolio project's lesson 12 both say is missing?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 5; The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 12.

choices.text: Already enough: a test that passes on its first run proves the fix works, which is what a bug fix needs
choices.why: A test that passes from its first run cannot be told apart from one that checks nothing. Both lessons say so.

choices.text: A second assistant reply, so that two different models agree that the test is right before it is kept
choices.why: Two replies are two draws from the same kind of guess. What decides is whether the test can see the bug, not how many models wrote it.

choices.text: Coverage of each line of the fix, which is what proves that a new test exercises the change
choices.why: Running a line is not the same as checking what it does. A test can cover the fix and assert nothing about `31/02`.

choices.text: The test run on the code before the fix, where it should fail; only then is it known to see the bug
choices.why: ai-dev lesson 5: a generated test should fail before the change it tests. Portfolio lesson 12: for a bug, the test comes first, and you see it fail.

prompt: A team turns on a bot that reviews every pull request with a model and posts an approval or a request for changes. Somebody proposes adding the bot's approval to the required checks on `main`. What do ai-dev lesson 4 and front-delivery lesson 3 say?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 4; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 3.

choices.text: Keep its comments for whoever decides; require the checks that are true or false, like tests and types
choices.why: ai-dev lesson 4 keeps the merge decision away from the bot, whose approval is a claim. front-delivery lesson 3's required check is a named job that passes or fails.

choices.text: Require it, since a check that nobody is obliged to wait for is a suggestion, and the bot reads every pull request
choices.why: That sentence is about checks that are true or false. A bot's approval is a list of hypotheses, and ai-dev lesson 4 showed three confident ones and the real bug missing.

choices.text: Require it on Fridays, when the human reviewers are least careful, and let people merge alone on other days
choices.why: Nothing in either lesson makes a gate depend on the day. The bot helps on late Friday pull requests by commenting, not by deciding.

choices.text: Turn the bot off, since a model misses an off-by-one at a boundary and its comments just cost tokens
choices.why: ai-dev lesson 4 says a good model does find local, mechanical findings like an off-by-one. The bot is useful as a first read.

prompt: The documentation search behind a help widget uses vector search. A colleague wants to switch to hybrid search "because it is always better". What did lesson 6's evaluation of twelve questions show?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 6.

choices.text: Keyword search won, 12 of 12, because each of the questions shared its words with the passages it needed
choices.why: Keyword search found 10 of 12, the lowest of the three. Lesson 6 showed a question that shares almost no words with its passage.

choices.text: 11 of 12, the same as vector search; it traded one miss for another, so measure on your own questions
choices.why: Vector search and hybrid search each found 11 of 12, and the miss moved. Whether hybrid helps a given widget is a measurement on its own questions, run on every change.

choices.text: Hybrid found 12 of 12, because merging two rankings always recovers whatever either one of them misses
choices.why: It did not. Merging two rankings fixed the identifier the vector search missed and lost a different question.

choices.text: Vector found 12 of 12 on its own, so hybrid adds cost for no gain and is not worth trying
choices.why: Vector search missed one, the error code E1042, which is why hybrid search exists. Lesson 6 does not rule it out; it measures it.

prompt: An agent's tools were described in a hurry. Match each flaw to the rule from lesson 7 that fixes it.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 7.

pairs.left: `manage_order(action, ...)`, which both looks up orders and refunds them
a description of `get_order` that never says its amounts are cents
pairs.right: say the units and the formats

pairs.left: a tool that answers with a 5,000-line log
pairs.right: results the model can use: plain and short

pairs.left: a failure answered with a stack trace
pairs.right: errors that say what to do

pairs.left: a lookup that changes nothing and carries no annotation saying so
pairs.right: read-only when it is, said in its annotations

right_distractors: a system prompt asking the model to choose tools carefully
more tools, so the model always finds one that fits

prompt: A checkout page's server calls `create_return` for a model, times out, and retries. The second attempt answers `R-1042-1` again instead of opening a second return, because the idempotency key comes from the ___, not from the model.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 8.

prompt: A help chat streams its reply into a `<div aria-live="polite">` that the script creates when the reply starts, and sets the div's text again on every piece that arrives. What is wrong with it for a screen-reader user? Choose all that apply.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 9; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 12.

choices.text: A region created at the moment its text arrives is usually read by nobody; it has to exist before
choices.why: front-quality lesson 12: a reader watches the live regions already in the page, so the region is made once and kept.

choices.text: Updated on every piece, it reads out fragments one after another instead of an answer
choices.why: ai-dev lesson 9: announce the reply once, when it is complete, or by sentence, so the reader has something to follow.

choices.text: It should be `role="alert"`, so that each piece interrupts what the reader is saying
choices.why: An alert interrupts and belongs to errors that cannot wait. A reply arriving is a status, and interrupting with every piece makes it worse.

choices.text: A live region is only read when it has the keyboard focus, so focus must move into the div
choices.why: A live region is read without the focus; that is what it is for. Moving the focus would also pull the user away from the question field.

choices.text: Streaming has to be turned off whenever a screen reader is detected, because the two cannot work together
choices.why: Nothing says so. The fix is in what the region is told and when, while the page still streams for whoever is watching.

prompt: Two models are tried for a feature that explains form errors to users. On the team's thirty cases, the cheaper one gets four wrong and the dearer one none. A colleague says the cheaper one wins on price. What does lesson 10 say?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 10.

choices.text: The cheaper one wins: output is dearer than input, so the model that writes less costs less overall
choices.why: Output is dearer than input, but that is about reply length on one model. It says nothing about a model that gives wrong answers.

choices.text: Not yet: price is decided by each provider's token counts, which have to be compared first
choices.why: Counting tokens per provider matters before a comparison to the dollar. It comes after knowing which models are good enough.

choices.text: The cheapest model that fails is the dearest: a wrong answer costs things no price list shows
choices.why: Lesson 10 puts it in those words. A wrong explanation becomes a support ticket or a lost customer, so the evaluation decides which models are candidates before prices are compared.

choices.text: The cheaper one wins if caching is turned on, since cached input costs a tenth and covers the four failures
choices.why: Caching lowers the price of a repeated prompt. It does not make a wrong answer right.

prompt: A product page asks a model to tidy up customer reviews and keep their formatting, then shows the result with `card.innerHTML = reply` and a comment: `// our own output, safe`. A review contained `<script>alert("hi")</script>`. What do ai-dev lesson 11 and front-quality lesson 9 say?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 11; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 9.

choices.text: Safe as written: a model rewrites what it reads, so a script tag in a review does not survive into its reply
choices.why: In ai-dev lesson 11 the model kept the tag, because it was asked to keep the markup. The reply copied what it read.

choices.text: Safe once the system prompt tells the model to drop scripts, since the instruction travels with every request
choices.why: Whether a model obeys an instruction is a matter of probability, not of rule. The defence that holds is in code, where the text becomes HTML.

choices.text: Unsafe only on browsers that run inline scripts, so a `Content-Security-Policy` header makes `innerHTML` the right choice
choices.why: Both lessons put the fix at the point where the string is turned into markup. A header does not change what `innerHTML` does with the string.

choices.text: Unsafe: the reply is text from outside, and `innerHTML` is a sink; escape it, or build the card with `textContent`
choices.why: ai-dev lesson 11: treat a model's reply like anything else that came from outside, because often it did. front-quality lesson 9 lists `innerHTML` as a sink with `textContent` as the safe way.

prompt: A CV says *I care about accessibility*. Which line under the portfolio project turns that claim into what portfolio lesson 1 calls evidence, written the way first-job lesson 4 asks?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 1; From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 4.

choices.text: Built a booking page for a dance school whose form works by keyboard alone, with labels and an axe check in CI
choices.why: It says what was done and for whom, what is now true, and how anybody can check it: lesson 4's *did, which, shown by*, and lesson 1's form with labels, a keyboard path and a check.

choices.text: Passionate about accessibility and inclusive design, with strong knowledge of WCAG 2.2, ARIA and modern CSS layout
choices.why: That is the same claim in more words. Lesson 4 cuts what every CV says, and lesson 1 says a claim with no evidence is the same on a CV and in a repository.

choices.text: Developed a responsive web application using HTML5, CSS3, TypeScript, Vite and the Vitest test runner, end to end
choices.why: A list of technologies describes a project that works and one that never ran. It answers a question nobody asked.

choices.text: Improved the accessibility of the project by 40%, measured against the usual industry benchmarks
choices.why: An interviewer asks where a number came from. With no measurement and no baseline, it costs more than no number at all.

prompt: A GitHub profile has five repositories from front-end tutorials and one finished project. What do portfolio lesson 2 and first-job lesson 5 say to do with the tutorials?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 2; From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 5.

choices.text: Delete them, since a reviewer who finds a tutorial anywhere in the list stops trusting the rest of the profile
choices.why: Nothing needs deleting. What hurts is a tutorial presented as your own work, or one competing with the project for the first click.

choices.text: Leave them unpinned with a one-line description saying which tutorial they follow, and pin the project
choices.why: Both lessons separate what exists from what is seen first. Pinned evidence, honest descriptions, and archived or private practice stop the tutorials competing.

choices.text: Pin the six of them, so the reviewer sees how much work went in before the project
choices.why: The reviewer samples. Six pinned repositories of equal weight are six chances to be judged by the weakest.

choices.text: Rename them after the project's problem, so they read as earlier versions of it
choices.why: A renamed tutorial is still the same tutorial, recognised by its file names, and lesson 2 says never to present one as your own.

prompt: Before sending a front-end portfolio link, which of these match what lesson 3 says the reviewer will do first? Choose all that apply.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 3; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 13.

choices.text: Open the live link on a phone
choices.why: Lesson 3: the live link first, and often on a phone.

choices.text: Narrow the layout to 320 pixels and see whether it still holds
choices.why: Lesson 3 checks the layout at 320 pixels, which front-quality lesson 13 explains: 1.4.10 *Reflow* asks for no sideways scrolling at that width.

choices.text: Use the form with the keyboard alone
choices.why: Lesson 3 asks whether the form can be used with the keyboard alone, in the browser's developer tools before any code.

choices.text: Count the green squares on the contribution graph
choices.why: The graph measures how often somebody pushed. Nothing in lesson 3's front-end paragraph looks at it.

choices.text: Read the dependency list in `package.json` before opening the page
choices.why: The code comes last in lesson 3's order, and there the reviewer looks at how state flows and whether the states exist.

choices.text: Check for a copy of a famous site, which shows the most skill
choices.why: Lesson 3 says a good project is an interface to real data with every state designed, not a copy of a famous site.

prompt: A friend asks for a page to manage the queue at her bike-repair shop. Match each question from lesson 4 to the part of the brief its answer fills.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 4.

pairs.left: How will you know it is working, a month from now?
Who would use it, and on what?
If it could do only one thing, which?

prompt: Lesson 7 reads loanbook's milestone dates off its tags: `v0.2.0` on 2026-06-15 and `v0.3.0` on 2026-06-29. The weekly note had worried about HTTPS. How many days did the deploy milestone take, from one tag to the next?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 7.

prompt: An interviewer for a team that works in two-week sprints asks how you organised your solo portfolio project. Which answer fits portfolio lesson 8 and git lesson 15?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 8; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 15.

choices.text: I ran two-week sprints alone, with planning, review and a burndown chart, to practise for a team like yours
choices.why: Done by one person, each ceremony answers a question nobody is asking. Lesson 8 calls it theatre.

choices.text: I estimated each card in story points so I could show you my velocity across the six weeks
choices.why: Velocity answers how much a team can take on in a sprint. Alone, you already know what you did last week.

choices.text: Three columns and one card in *doing* at a time, because sprint ceremonies need more than one person
choices.why: Lesson 8 gives that sentence for the interview: knowing the vocabulary, and a decision with its reason. git lesson 15 says the WIP limit is what stops a board becoming a list.

choices.text: No board: a solo project has nobody to coordinate, so writing tasks down would be theatre
choices.why: Lesson 8 keeps a board for one person, because its job is to remember what you would otherwise forget.

prompt: The working tree holds a fix to `app.py`, its test in `test_app.py`, and a `print("DEBUG body", body)` left in `app.py`. Put lesson 9's steps to a commit that holds the fix and its test and nothing else in order.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 9.
items: `git add -p app.py`, answering `y` to the fix's hunk and `n` to the debug line's
`git diff`, which now lists only the debug line and the unstaged test
`git restore app.py`, which throws the debug line away
`git add test_app.py`
`git commit`, with a body saying the test came first and failed
trap: The likeliest slip is restoring `app.py` before staging the fix. `git restore` puts the working file back to the stage, so with nothing staged it throws away the fix along with the debug line.

prompt: You are the only reviewer of your own portfolio pull request. Which of these give the distance lesson 10 asks for, or the check ai-dev lesson 4 would accept? Choose all that apply.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 10; AI in Development, lesson 4.

choices.text: Reading the diff the next morning instead of five minutes after writing it
choices.why: Time is the first of lesson 10's three kinds of distance: the gap lets you see the code instead of the intention.

choices.text: Reading it on the hosting site's pull-request page rather than in the editor
choices.why: A different view: the change looks the way a reviewer will see it.

choices.text: Reading the tests first, then checking that the code does what they claim
choices.why: A different order, which is what a reviewer does.

choices.text: Asking an assistant to approve the diff and merging when it says it looks good
choices.why: ai-dev lesson 4 keeps the merge decision away from a bot: its approval is a claim, and silence about a bug reads like approval.

choices.text: Rereading it in the editor straight away, while what you meant is still fresh
choices.why: That freshness is the problem. You remember what you meant, and memory fills in what the diff does not say.

prompt: A shop page lists forty products, each with a button labelled *Add to cart*. axe reports no problems. What does a keyboard walk like lesson 13's find, and why did axe not?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 13; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 10.

choices.text: No problem: forty buttons with a name each is the floor, and the walk just repeats what axe already checked
choices.why: In lesson 13 the walk found what axe passed. Every name was correct and none was useful.

choices.text: That the buttons fail contrast at 4.5:1, which axe skips on repeated elements
choices.why: Contrast is one of the things axe does decide. The problem here is what the names say.

choices.text: That forty buttons are too many stops, so all but the first should get `tabindex="-1"`
choices.why: Taking buttons out of the tab order makes them unreachable by keyboard. The fix is in their names.

choices.text: Forty stops all called *Add to cart*; each needs a name saying what it acts on, which axe cannot judge
choices.why: Lesson 13's *Borrower, Lend, Borrower, Lend* became *Lend Projector 1 to*. front-quality lesson 10 lists whether a name describes what a control does among the questions a machine cannot answer.

prompt: A portfolio single-page app calls a weather service whose only key grants the whole account. Its author follows portfolio lesson 14 and reads the key from an environment variable, `VITE_WEATHER_KEY`, at build time. Why is that not enough here?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 14; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 2.

choices.text: The build copies it into a file every visitor downloads; an account-wide key belongs on a server
choices.why: front-delivery lesson 2: if the browser has it, the person using the browser has it, and a service with one key only gets treated as secret. Lesson 14's environment protects a value the server reads at run time.

choices.text: It is enough as long as `.env` is in `.gitignore`, which is the half of lesson 14 that matters
choices.why: Ignoring the file keeps the value out of the repository. The bundle is a second place, built from the same variable, and it is public by design.

choices.text: It is enough if the variable is read with square brackets and no default, so a missing key fails at once
choices.why: That rule makes a missing secret fail loudly. It does nothing about a present one copied into the page.

choices.text: It fails because the pre-commit hook does not recognise `VITE_`, so the key is committed by accident
choices.why: The key is not in a commit at all here. It is in the built JavaScript, where no hook looks.

prompt: A portfolio site will live on a free static host. Which of these does lesson 15 say to check on the provider's own current pages before trusting the free tier? Choose all that apply.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 1.

choices.text: whether it sleeps when idle, so the first visit is slow
choices.why: One of lesson 15's five: a sleeping tier makes a reviewer wait on the first click.

choices.text: whether it expires after a trial period
choices.why: Also one of the five; a free tier that ends turns the link in the CV into an error.

choices.text: how you leave, since a portfolio outlives most free tiers
choices.why: The fifth check. front-delivery lesson 1 says the same thing from the other side: a free plan is somebody else's business decision.

choices.text: the limits this course quotes for each of the four hosts
choices.why: Neither course quotes any. front-delivery lesson 1 explains why: a number written in October 2026 would be wrong before you read it.

choices.text: which host has the most stars on GitHub
choices.why: Popularity is not on the list. The five checks are about what happens to your site.

prompt: A portfolio README's *Run it* section says `npm ci && npm run dev`, and both work on the author's laptop. How do portfolio lesson 16 and front-delivery lesson 3 say to find out whether the claim holds?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 16; Deployment, Design Systems and GraphQL, lesson 3.

choices.text: Run the two commands again on the laptop after deleting `node_modules`, which removes everything that was installed
choices.why: The laptop still has every variable you ever set and every file you never committed. Lesson 16 calls your own machine the worst place for this test.

choices.text: Clone the repository onto a machine with nothing of the project on it and type exactly what the README says
choices.why: Lesson 16 runs the README cold on a machine built from nothing; front-delivery lesson 3 shows why: a file your computer has and the repository does not fails only on a clean copy.

choices.text: Ask a friend to read the README and say whether the steps look complete
choices.why: Reading is not running. The step you do out of habit and forgot to write down is invisible to a reader too.

choices.text: Add a badge saying *build passing*, so a reviewer sees it works without running anything
choices.why: A badge reports what CI ran. It does not test what the README tells a person to type.

prompt: Which `alt` text fits the screenshot at the top of a study planner's README, by portfolio lesson 17 and front-quality lesson 12?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 17; Testing, Security and Accessibility, lesson 12.

choices.text: `alt="Screenshot of my project"`
choices.why: It names the kind of file and says nothing it shows. Lesson 12 also says not to start with *image of*, since the reader already says *image*.

choices.text: `alt=""`, because the README's paragraph above already says what the project is
choices.why: Empty `alt` marks decoration. The screenshot is the first evidence a reviewer sees, so it carries meaning.

choices.text: `alt="The planner: three sessions this week, one course marked done"`
choices.why: It says in one line what the picture shows, which lesson 17 also uses as a test of the picture, and it is what the image is for, which is lesson 12's rule.

choices.text: `alt="planner-2026-10-03.png"`, so that the file can be found again later
choices.why: A file name is what a reader falls back on when `alt` is missing, and it says nothing about what the picture shows.

prompt: Your two-minute project script runs to two minutes forty when you time it aloud. Where does lesson 19 say to cut?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 19.

choices.text: From the problem, since the listener can read whose problem it was in the README
choices.why: The problem is already short, about twenty-five seconds, and it is what makes the listener care.

choices.text: Leave it: speak faster, since the content was right and the pace was what ran slow
choices.why: Lesson 19 says the fix is not to speak faster. It is to cut.

choices.text: From the result, ending on the decision so the listener remembers the hard part
choices.why: The result is short already and it ends on something the listener can open, which is the evidence.

choices.text: From the decision: keep the choice and its reason, and cut the second reason, the history and the alternatives
choices.why: The decision is what grows, because every detail feels essential to the person who made it. What is cut is what lesson 20's questions will ask for anyway.

prompt: An advert for a junior front-end role says you would be the only person responsible for the whole product, from design to deploy. What does lesson 1 say to do with that line?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 1.

choices.text: Ask in the screening call who you would learn from: it reads as a senior role with a junior salary
choices.why: Lesson 1 names this line as one that deserves a second look rather than a pass, and the question to ask is who would teach you.

choices.text: Treat it as a nice-to-have, like the fourth framework, and apply as you would to any advert
choices.why: It is not one more tool. It changes what the job is, and lesson 1 picks it out for that reason.

choices.text: Skip the advert, since a company that writes it has told you it will not hire a junior
choices.why: Lesson 1 does not say to skip it. It says to ask, and the answer decides.

choices.text: Rewrite the CV to show you have done each part of a product alone before
choices.why: The CV argues for the work the advert describes. Claiming to have run a whole product alone does not answer the question the line raises.

prompt: Your contribution graph is empty for the six weeks of your portfolio project, though you pushed every week. `git log --format='%an <%ae>'` shows on every commit the personal address you typed the day you installed git, which your GitHub account does not have. What do first-job lesson 5 and portfolio lesson 18 point to?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 5; The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 18.

choices.text: The graph counts merged pull requests rather than commits, so each of those commits needs a pull request of its own
choices.why: The graph counts commits made with an address linked to your account. Pull requests are not the issue here.

choices.text: GitHub links them to nobody; switch `user.email` to the no-reply one so the next ones count
choices.why: Lesson 5: make sure your commits count by committing with an e-mail GitHub links to your account. Lesson 18 sets up the no-reply address for exactly that, and before the first push.

choices.text: Rewrite the commits with the new address and force-push `main`, so the six weeks turn green
choices.why: `main` on GitHub is a branch a reviewer may have cloned, and the one rule of tidying is to rewrite only what nobody else has.

choices.text: Push a few empty commits each day for the next weeks, so that the graph matches what the CV says
choices.why: Lesson 5 says empty commits to keep the graph green are visible to anybody who clicks a square, and read exactly as they are.

prompt: Lesson 8 counts its invented tracker's stages with `cut -d, -f5 applications.csv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`. Adding up the counts it printed, how many applications does the file hold?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 8.

prompt: Lesson 9 says to write down the people you know, in a given order, before asking anybody for a referral. Put the list in that order.
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 9.
items: people you studied with, on any course, who now work somewhere
teachers and instructors
people from previous jobs, in any field
family and neighbours, asked plainly
people at the companies on your list whom you have never met
trap: The likeliest slip is starting with the strangers at the companies you want. Lesson 9 puts them last, as the hardest group, and the message it writes is for them.

prompt: A take-home asks for a booking form that refuses a date in the past, in about three hours. Which hand-in fits first-job lesson 13 and portfolio lesson 12?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 13; The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 12.

choices.text: Each brief requirement plus a dark theme and animations, sent two days late because they took longer than planned
choices.why: A late, perfect submission is usually worse than an on-time one, and an extra feature on top reads as not having read the brief.

choices.text: The form with tests on every component and a coverage report at 95%, and no note, since the tests explain the choices
choices.why: Lesson 13 asks for a note: what you did, what you chose and why, what you would do with more time. And one test that fails when the rule is removed says more than coverage.

choices.text: Brief first, a README run on a clean machine, a short note, and a test seen failing with the rule removed
choices.why: That is lesson 13's list. Portfolio lesson 12 adds how to know the test guards the rule: remove the rule and watch the right test fail.

choices.text: Half the brief done perfectly and the rest left out silently, so the reviewer judges just the polished work
choices.why: When the time runs out, stop and say what is missing in the notes. A silent gap reads worse than an honest one.

prompt: A recruiter who is not technical opens the screening call with *tell me about yourself*. Which answer follows first-job lesson 11, which borrows its shape from portfolio lesson 19?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 11; The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 19.

choices.text: A walk through the stack of the portfolio project, from the framework to the CSS, to show the depth behind the CV
choices.why: The person checking is not technical, and lesson 19 keeps the technology inside the decision, where it has a reason.

choices.text: The story of how you first got interested in computers, so the recruiter sees motivation before the CV

choices.text: A short apology for having no job in IT yet, followed by the list of courses you have finished

prompt: *Tell me about a time you failed.* Which answer has the shape first-job lesson 15 asks for, with its material taken from a retrospective like portfolio lesson 21's?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 15; The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 21.

choices.text: I estimated the rules milestone at three and a half days; it took five, because I had not counted the error handling. Now I estimate each milestone with its should items.
choices.why: A STAR story with an honest result, and the last sentence is what changed. The facts come first and the conclusion after, as the retrospective writes them.

choices.text: Honestly, I tend to be a perfectionist, so my projects take longer because I keep improving them until they are right.
choices.why: That is the disguised strength lesson 15 says interviewers have heard thousands of times. It has no failure in it.

choices.text: The deploy failed because the free tier changed its limits without warning, which nobody could have predicted.
choices.why: An answer that blames something else is the other one lesson 15 says fails. And it says nothing about what you changed.

choices.text: We missed a deadline once, but the team pulled together and in the end everything was delivered and the client was happy.
choices.why: No failure of yours and no action of yours: *we*, not *I*, and a result with nothing learned in it.

prompt: Your first ticket at work is to fix a form label that a screen reader announces wrongly. What does first-job lesson 20 want from it, with the habits of portfolio lesson 10?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 20; The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 10.

choices.text: Fix the other labels on the page while you are there, so that the first change shows the team how much you can do
choices.why: A pull request that quietly fixes several unrelated things is harder to review. Lesson 10 opens a card for what it finds and fixes it separately.

choices.text: Small, finished properly and visible: what and why in the message, a self-review first, and *done* said aloud
choices.why: Lesson 20: small, finished properly at the team's standard, and visible. The self-review before the review is lesson 10's habit.

choices.text: Ask for a larger first task instead, since a single label is too small to show the team what you already know
choices.why: Lesson 20 says the opposite: a large first task that drags for three weeks is the worst start.

choices.text: Merge it quietly without mentioning it to anyone, since announcing a one-line fix to the team reads as boasting
choices.why: Visible is one of the three rules: say it is done where the team says such things, as the normal end of a task.

prompt: The evidence line at the top of your CV links to the portfolio repository. By first-job lesson 3 and portfolio lesson 16, what should the README's first screen show the person who clicks?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 3; The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 16.

choices.text: The installation steps, so a reviewer can run it before deciding anything
choices.why: Installation steps for a project the reader cannot yet picture are what lesson 16 moves below the first screen.

choices.text: A row of badges and a table of contents, so the reader sees the project is maintained and organised
choices.why: Lesson 16 keeps both off the first screen: they push the paragraph and the picture below the fold.

choices.text: One paragraph saying what it is and for whom, a picture of it working, and the live address
choices.why: The same job as the CV's ten seconds: what this is and whether it works. Lesson 16 puts a live address in the second line, as a link.

choices.text: A paragraph about you and why you built it, since the CV has already said what the project is
choices.why: Lesson 16 sends a paragraph about yourself to the profile. The README is about the project.
